editorial.note: This is an archetypal image of an affluent Dutch citizen at the beginning of the 17th century: confident – even a touch pompous – and fashionably dressed, but without undue excess.
Widow Sara de Bie was the second wife of Johannes Lutma, whom she married in 1638. At the time it was a rarity for an artist to be portrayed with his wife.
Jaapgen Caerlsdr is 70 years old in this portrait. Hailing from a distinguished lineage, she was the daughter of a Leiden glazier.

Maria van Strijp was a member of a wealthy Haarlem family active in the flourishing textile trade. Her jewellery and black dress sumptuously trimmed with lace are far more valuable than this painting of her.

editorial.note: Sir Thomas Gresham (1519–1579) was the leading English merchant in Antwerp and also the English king’s financial agent in the Low Countries. He and his wife, Anne Fernely, are expensively, yet soberly dressed.

151697.title: Portrait of Haesje Jacobsdr van Cleyburg
151697.creator: Rembrandt van Rijn

editorial.note: Rembrandt travelled to Rotterdam to portray the brewing couple Haesje van Cleyburg and Dirck Pesser, who were part of the city’s Remonstrant elite. While at first glance her attire may seem modest, in reality it was quite lavish.

151701.creator: Rembrandt van Rijn

editorial.note: The sitter is likely the 20-year-old Maria Trip. She hailed from an extremely wealthy family involved in the arms trade.

151791.title: Portrait of an Old Lady, possibly Elisabeth Bas
151791.creator: attributed to Ferdinand Bol

editorial.note: This portrait may depict Elisabeth Bas. Like many seafarers’ wives, Bas managed the provisioning of the fleet of her husband, Admiral Jochem Swartenhondt.

Feyntje van Steenkiste hailed from a prosperous family active in the Haarlem textile industry, a connection shared by her husband Lucas de Clercq and his family. Their union strengthened the business ties between their respective families.
Maritge Vooght grew up in a Haarlem family business of brewers. She married Pieter Olycan at the age of 18. Their union allowed him to hold high positions and he became co-heir to the brewery.

152178.title: Portrait of a Woman with a Squirrel
152178.creator: attributed to Francesco Montemezzano

editorial.note: Attributed to Francesco Montemezzano (c. 1540 - after 1602). Portrait of a Woman with a Squirrel c. 1570. From the Otto Lanz collection, 1948.

Maria Rey and Roelof Meulenaer married in 1649. This may have been the reason for having both of their portraits painted. Maria and Roelof’s black clothing might look sober, but in fact it is made of silk and was thus very expensive.
Nicolaes Eliasz called Pickenoy (1590/91-1654/56). Portrait of Maria Joachimsdr. Swartenhont, wife of Maerten Rey, 1627. Panel. Bequest of Jonkheer J.S.H. van de Poll, 1880.

Catharina Behaghel was a member of Antwerp’s wealthy bourgeoisie. Her clothes and accessories, such as the fan, reflect her status. She was probably pregnant when she and her husband were portrayed by Jordaens.
Magdalena de Cuyper is portrayed as a widow, with a black cap, a prayer book, and a flowering tulip. The latter two objects symbolize her piety, and transience.
Nicolaes Eliasz, named Pickenoy (1588 - 1650/56). Johanna Le Maire, wife of Pieter van Son, 1622. Purchase made possible by the SponsorBingo Lottery.

Marten and Oopjen are the only couple that Rembrandt painted life-size, standing, and at full-length. Marten’s father came to Amsterdam from Antwerp as a Protestant refugee. He made his fortune as the owner of a sugar refinery.
Oopjen was the eldest of three daughters of an old, affluent Amsterdam family. She sat to Rembrandt one year after her wedding with Marten. She was 23, and pregnant with her first child.
This touching and intimate portrait was made towards the end of Liotard’s first sojourn in the Netherlands.
